title: Beginner's mind
hook: the expert sees few possibilities. the beginner sees many.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zhaozhou's mu, one syllable that doesn't fit the question. Your line was mu. Did a quick yes or no get a breath of mu first? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

Shoelaces. Somebody tied a pair this morning without a single thought about loops or tension or which hand goes where. Now watch a small child do it for the first time. Tongue out. Every loop is an event. The lace slips, and it's fascinating. Same shoes, same laces, two completely different experiences of the same knot. The adult is faster, and that's useful. But somewhere along the way, the knot stopped being interesting. Zen has a name for the child's side of that scene, and it treats it as something worth practicing on purpose. Today's word is the mind that's new at things.
screen: `A KNOT TIED WITHOUT A THOUGHT.` → `A CHILD'S FIRST KNOT.` → `THE MIND THAT'S NEW AT THINGS.`

segments.voice: Shoshin is the Japanese word usually put into English as beginner's mind. First, the line that carried it. Shunryu Suzuki, a Japanese Soto Zen teacher who taught in San Francisco, opened a collection of his talks, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, with an idea that can be paraphrased like this: a beginner's mind holds many possibilities, and an expert's holds only a few. Second, what the expert loses. Knowing how something goes is a kind of shortcut. You stop looking because you already know. That saves time. It also quietly closes doors. The expert's mind is full, and a full mind has a hard time noticing what's actually in front of it. Third, what it isn't. Beginner's mind isn't pretending to know nothing, and it isn't throwing skill away. A beginner's mind can belong to someone who's sat zazen every day for decades. Suzuki's point, in paraphrase, was that the practice is to keep the beginner's mind, not to graduate from it. Fourth, why Zen cares. Zen practice repeats itself on purpose: the same cushion, the same posture, the same breath. Without beginner's mind, that would be a rut. With it, each sitting can be a first sitting. And it ties back to the koans of the last two days. A koan resists the expert. Mu won't open for someone who already knows the answer. On an ordinary Tuesday, beginner's mind might be as plain as listening to a friend tell a story you've heard before, and actually hearing it.
screen: `MANY POSSIBILITIES, OR FEW.` · `THE EXPERT STOPS LOOKING.` · `NOT FORGETTING YOUR SKILL.` · `EACH SITTING, A FIRST SITTING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet something familiar as a beginner. Hold out one of your hands, palm up, and look at it as if you'd never seen a hand before. The lines. The color. How the fingers bend, and in which places. Then close your eyes and feel it from the inside: warmth, tingling, weight. When the mind says, it's just my hand, I know this, notice that voice, and look again. If you'd rather, take one breath as if it were the first breath you'd ever taken. The bell holds the time.
Shoshin. Beginner's mind. Meeting even the familiar with open eyes, without throwing away what you know. Today's word.

Your line: beginner's mind. Today, pick one thing you do on autopilot, making coffee, a commute, a familiar conversation, and do it once as if it were your first time. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Zen teachers speak of beginner's mind as a way to approach each sitting and each ordinary task freshly, and students are encouraged to keep it however long they have practiced.

make it the usual way, but notice it as if for the first time.
